presentingComplaint: Reduced urine output and confusion for 1 day, on background of 3 days of fever and cough
history: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents with a 3-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive breathlessness, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia treated empirically as an outpatient with oral gentamicin-containing eye drops for conjunctivitis and, more relevantly, was started on IV piperacillin-tazobactam and empirical gentamicin 2 days ago after admission for severe CAP with septic features. Over the last 24 hours his family notes he has passed very little urine (only ~150 mL in the last day) and has become increasingly drowsy and confused. There is no prior history of chronic kidney disease; his baseline creatinine 3 months ago was 0.9 mg/dL. No history of contrast exposure, no NSAID use, no diarrhea or vomiting to suggest volume depletion. No known obstructive uropathy symptoms.
examination: Lethargic, mildly disoriented to time. Warm peripheries initially with subsequent cool extremities. Dry mucous membranes are absent (patient appears euvolemic to mildly hypervolemic with bibasal crackles). No rash. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no palpable bladder. No flank tenderness. Bilateral basal crepitations on chest auscultation consistent with underlying pneumonia. No peripheral edema at presentation.

labs.urinalysis: muddy brown granular casts, renal tubular epithelial cells, no significant proteinuria, no dysmorphic RBCs

imaging: Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys bilaterally, no hydronephrosis, no obstruction, mildly increased cortical echogenicity
Chest X-ray: right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia
microbiology: Blood cultures pending at time of AKI onset (drawn on admission, prior culture growing Escherichia coli sensitive to piperacillin-tazobactam and gentamicin, reported after 48h)
Sputum culture: Escherichia coli, same susceptibility pattern as blood isolate
differentialDiagnoses: Acute tubular necrosis (sepsis-associated and aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity)
Contrast-induced nephropathy (no contrast history, less likely)
finalDiagnosis: Acute kidney injury due to acute tubular necrosis, multifactorial (sepsis-associated hypoperfusion plus aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity)
citations: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury 2012
stewardship: Continue source-directed therapy for the underlying E. coli bacteremic pneumonia per culture sensitivities (piperacillin-tazobactam); discontinue gentamicin immediately given nephrotoxicity and achievable de-escalation to a beta-lactam alone; renally dose all antimicrobials to actual GFR, avoid further nephrotoxins, and monitor levels/renal function closely if any aminoglycoside continuation were unavoidable.
contraindications: Avoid further aminoglycoside dosing given established nephrotoxicity
Avoid NSAIDs and iodinated contrast unless absolutely necessary
Avoid ACE inhibitors/ARBs and potassium-sparing agents until AKI resolves
Renally adjust all renally-cleared drugs (including piperacillin-tazobactam) to current kidney function
edgeCases: If oliguria progresses to anuria with refractory hyperkalemia, fluid overload, or refractory acidosis, urgent renal replacement therapy is indicated regardless of creatinine trend
Differentiating ATN from prerenal azotemia can be difficult in early sepsis; FeNa and muddy brown casts favor established ATN here
Consider AIN if eosinophilia, rash, or fever pattern change after piperacillin-tazobactam exposure, though urinalysis here is more consistent with ATN
This presentation (aki) is captured in the diagnosable disease set as a discrete nephrology diagnosis rather than as a specific ATN subtype; acceptableIds therefore map to the general AKI entity
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag this as sepsis-associated AKI with superimposed aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity, recommend immediate cessation of the nephrotoxic agent, renal dosing of remaining antimicrobials, and close monitoring for RRT indications (refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, fluid overload, uremic complications).
expectedNextQuestions: What is the trend in urine output over the next 6-12 hours despite fluid resuscitation?
Is there a need for renal replacement therapy based on the AEIOU criteria (acidosis, electrolyte, intoxication, overload, uremia)?
Has the aminoglycoside been discontinued and can the beta-lactam be renally dosed appropriately?
Is there any evidence of AIN (eosinophilia, rash, drug fever pattern) that would warrant a nephrology biopsy discussion?
expectedInvestigations: Serum potassium and bicarbonate (arterial or venous blood gas)
CK to exclude rhabdomyolysis as contributing cause
